output:
# My van nearly caught fire. Here's what was wrong with it.

Not a fun post, sorry. No before-and-afters today.

On Wednesday, October 28, around 2:15 in the afternoon, I was parked in a client's driveway in Bedford drying a Bernese named Moose. Dryer on high, which with a Berner is the only setting. I smelled hot plastic and figured it was the dryer motor, because they get a smell when they're working hard and Moose is a lot of dog. I kept going for longer than I'd like to admit.

Then I saw smoke coming out of the bench seat. The bench seat is where my batteries live.

I killed the battery switch, got Moose out the side door still damp (he was thrilled, honestly, best groom of his life), and grabbed the extinguisher. I gave the battery compartment a bit of a blast. I'm not even sure I needed to, since the power was already off. When I looked properly, the metal connector on the end of the positive cable was black and the cable's plastic jacket had melted back about 3 cm from it.

Everyone is fine. Moose is fine. I'm fine in the sense that I'm not burned. Moose's mom came out with a coffee and sat with me on her front steps while I shook, and that dog is getting a free groom at some point whether she likes it or not.

The van is off the road for weeks. More on that at the bottom.

I'm writing this up properly because a lot of you reading this are groomers with vans, or about to be. One of you (hi Tasha) is about to pay a deposit to the same builder who did mine. So this is everything I learned, in the plainest language I can manage.

Big disclaimer before I start: I am not an electrician. I groom dogs. Everything technical in here is what an electrician showed me and explained to me, written down right after she left. If something in this post makes you nervous about your own van, good, get a professional to look at it. Please don't rewire anything because a dog groomer's blog told you to.

## My setup

My van was built in spring 2025 by Coastline Van Fitouts (Darren). The electrical side is:

- a 3000 watt inverter
- two 200Ah lithium batteries
- a 12 volt system

If you're new to this, the batteries put out 12 volts and your dryer wants regular household power. The inverter is the box that turns one into the other. Everything your dryer uses has to travel from the batteries to the inverter through one fat cable. That cable is the one that melted.

## What the electrician found

Priya from Sackville Marine Electric came out to look at it. She found three separate problems, and any one of them would have been bad on its own.

### 1. The cable was way too small

The cable from my batteries to my inverter was 4 AWG. Priya says for a 3000 watt inverter on a 12 volt system it should have been 2/0.

Cable sizes are confusing because the numbers go backwards. A smaller number is a thicker cable. Once you get past 1 you're into 1/0, 2/0 and so on, which are thicker again. 2/0 (people say "two aught") has roughly three times as much copper in it as 4 gauge. So mine wasn't a little undersized, it was about a third of what it should have been.

Here's why that matters, and this is the one bit of math I'm going to make you do:

**watts ÷ volts = amps**

Amps is how much electricity is flowing through the cable. More amps needs a thicker cable, the same way more water needs a bigger pipe.

My dryer pulls about 1800 to 2000 watts. Divide that by 12 volts and you get 150 to 165-ish amps. Sometimes the water heater kicks in at the same time and it goes higher. If the inverter is working at its full 3000 watts, that's 250 amps.

So on a normal day my cable was carrying somewhere between 150 and 250 amps. Through a cable about a third the size it should have been, for hours a day, since spring 2025. It got hot every single time I dried a dog. I just couldn't see it.

### 2. The connector on the end was crimped badly

The metal ring on the end of a battery cable is called a lug. It's supposed to be squeezed onto the cable with a proper crimping tool, which presses it evenly all the way around until the lug and the copper strands are basically one solid piece.

The lug on my positive cable had been crimped with something like pliers or a hammer. It was squashed on, not properly crimped.

The reason that matters is that with a bad crimp, all that current has to squeeze through whatever little bits of metal are actually touching, and that spot heats up. That's exactly where mine burned. The lug was black and the jacket melted back from that end.

I never saw it, because there was a nice neat piece of heat shrink over the top hiding the whole thing.

### 3. The fuse couldn't have saved me

I do have a main fuse. It's a 300 amp ANL fuse. Two problems with it.

First, it was mounted about 90 cm away from the battery. Priya said it should be within about 18 cm. The fuse only protects the cable after it. Everything between the battery and the fuse is connected straight to the battery with nothing to stop it if something goes wrong. I had 90 cm of that.

Second, and it took me a minute to get this one, the fuse never had a reason to blow. A 300 amp fuse blows when more than 300 amps goes through it. My cable was cooking at 150 to 250. As far as the fuse was concerned, nothing was wrong. A fuse only helps if the cable it's protecting can handle more than the fuse can, and mine couldn't come close.

The repair includes moving the fuse and switching to a different type called a Class T. The way I understand it, lithium batteries can dump an enormous amount of current if something shorts out, and a Class T is built to actually stop that.

### And one that's on me

There's no smoke detector in the back of my van. There's just the one in the cab that came with the van. I smelled it and then saw it, and I got lucky that I was standing right there when it happened. There will be a detector back there before I groom another dog in that van.

## The photos

I think this is what really got to me. Priya pulled up my damage photos next to thermal camera pictures of her own van running the same kind of load. A thermal camera shows heat as colour. In hers, the cables and connections barely get warm, and the pictures are boring. In mine you're looking at a black lug and melted plastic.

It's the same job and the same kind of power, and the difference is wild. That's what a correctly sized cable and a proper crimp look like next to what I had.

## Tidy is not the same as right

I trusted my build because it looked tidy. The cables were all run neatly, there was heat shrink on everything, things were labelled, and nothing was dangling. I looked in that compartment more than once and thought, yep, that's professional.

Tidy is not the same as right. I had no idea what size the cable should be or how far the fuse should be from the battery. I didn't know those were questions. I'm guessing a lot of you don't either, so here's what I'd do.

## A checklist you can do yourself, power off

This is looking only. You're not fixing or undoing anything. You're collecting information to take to an electrician.

**Before you start:** turn off your battery switch and unplug from shore power if you're plugged in. Take off rings, bracelets and watches. The battery switch does not make the battery terminals safe. They're always live, so no tools in there at all, and nothing metal anywhere near them.

1. **Find your inverter and read the label.** Write down the watts (1000, 2000, 3000, whatever). Also find out if your system is 12 volt or 24 volt. If you don't know, your builder paperwork or the battery labels should say.

2. **Do the math.** Watts ÷ volts = amps. That's the most your big cable might have to carry.

3. **Read the cable.** Find the thick cable going from the batteries to the inverter. The size is usually printed along the jacket, something like "4 AWG" or "2/0". Write it down and take a photo.

4. **Look up your inverter's manual.** Google the model number. The manual will tell you what cable size and what fuse the manufacturer wants. Compare that to what you wrote down in step 3. If they don't match, that's your first question for an electrician.

5. **Find the main fuse.** Follow the positive cable from the battery until you hit it. Write down the type and the number on it. Then measure how far it is from the battery along the cable. Priya's number was within about 18 cm. Mine was 90. If you can't find a fuse at all, stop here and call someone.

6. **Look hard at the ends of the cables.** You're looking for anything brown, black, shiny, bubbled or melted. Check whether the heat shrink has gone a funny colour and whether the cable jacket looks like it's pulled back from the lug. Hands only, gently wiggle the cable where it goes into the lug. It shouldn't move at all.

7. **Smell it.** I'm serious. Hot plastic has a smell and it hangs around. If your battery compartment smells like that, something has been getting hot.

8. **Check your safety stuff.** Is there a smoke detector in the grooming area and not just the cab? Is your extinguisher somewhere you can grab it in two seconds? Can you reach your battery switch without putting your arm into the place the smoke would be coming from?

Take photos of everything. If any of it looks off, send the photos to an electrician and don't use the van for heavy loads until they've answered.

## Buy a $40 thermometer

Everyone with a van should own a cheap infrared thermometer. It's the point-and-shoot kind with the little laser dot, and I got mine for 40 bucks at Canadian Tire.

This one is a power-on check, so no touching anything. Run your dryer on high for ten or fifteen minutes like you would on a normal groom. Then open the battery compartment and point the thermometer at the cable, at each end of the cable, and at the fuse. Shiny metal throws the reading off, so aim at the cable jacket or the heat shrink right beside the lug.

I don't have a magic number for you, because I'm not qualified to give one. What Priya's photos taught me is that a healthy setup is boring. Everything is about the same temperature and barely warmer than the air around it. What you're hunting for is one spot that's way hotter than everything near it. If you find one, turn everything off, write down the reading, and call an electrician.

If I'd owned one of these in the spring, I would have caught this in the first week.

## Before you pay anyone a deposit

Tasha, this part is for you, but it goes for anybody getting a van built by any builder.

Before you hand over money, ask for these in writing:

- What size cable will run between the batteries and the inverter? Does that match what the inverter manual calls for?
- What's the main fuse? I mean the type, the amp rating, and how far from the battery it will be mounted.
- What tool do you use to crimp the big lugs? Can I get photos of the crimps before the heat shrink goes on?
- Is there a smoke detector in the grooming area?

Then take those answers to an electrician before you sign. It's a lot cheaper than the repair I'm paying for. A builder who knows their stuff will have these answers off the top of their head and won't be offended that you asked. If someone gets weird about writing down a cable size, that tells you something.

## About my builder

I'm not trying to trash anyone here, so I'm sticking to facts. Coastline Van Fitouts built my van in spring 2025. The cable, the crimp and the fuse placement are what Priya found, and I have photos of all of it. I've sent Darren three texts and an email since it happened and haven't heard back yet. If I do, I'll update this post and tell you what he said. You can decide for yourselves.

## Where I'm at

The repair quote is $4,200. That covers rewiring the main cable runs, a new fuse block and the Class T fuse. It's three weeks minimum because parts are on order.

I've cancelled 31 appointments so far. If you're one of them, I'm so sorry, and I'll be in touch to rebook the second I have a date. Insurance says "maybe." The adjuster is coming Thursday.

I'm not going to pretend I'm okay about it. I'm scared. That van is my whole income and rent is due on the 1st. I keep doing the math on the 31 appointments and then making myself stop.

But I keep coming back to the fact that it happened in a driveway, in the daytime, with me standing right there and a dog who thought the whole thing was a great adventure. It could have gone differently, and I got lucky.

So go look at your van. Do the checklist, buy the thermometer, and get someone qualified to look at anything that seems off.

I'll post again when the van's back.

---

A few things to check before you post:

- **The date:** your notes say October 28, which is two weeks back now, so I used the date instead of "last week."
- **Thursday:** make sure that's still the right day for the adjuster when this goes up.
- **Bits I added:** the backwards cable numbering, why a Class T suits lithium, the inverter manual tip and the warning that battery terminals stay live are standard, but they weren't in your notes. It's worth running them past Priya, since you're naming her.
